rv.q: This subversive comedy is now a posh panto, directed by Max Webster.
Every nook and cranny of this brightly lit (thanks for the gaudiness, Jon Clark) production is ornate.
With its dazzle, joy and original anarchic spirit of pantomime, this is the most stylish festive show in town.
I loved it because it honours Wilde’s wit but also his radicalism and his embrace of artifice.
This is a big success, oh yes it is.
History is worn oh-so-lightly here, and it’s impossible not to get swept up in the fun.

Which we very much are: handing the story over to its own cackling id and an ensemble of very beautiful, very charismatic, very funny actors, this Earnest could stand to be 15 minutes shorter but is otherwise a pure blast.
This gorgeous, joyously out-there staging feels almost like payback.
This is comic acting of the highest order.
Over nearly three hours, this gossamer creation gets stretched very thin indeed, especially at the denouement, which here feels interminable.

And while I don’t want to be a party-pooper, a slight sense of exhaustion set in watching his concertedly exuberant, subtext-declaring Earnest, which amply suits the gaiety of the panto season and has its moments but isn’t really one for the annals.
It’s an utter delight, the perfect Christmas choice.
This is where you’ll find pure magic theatre this Christmas.
Fun, fabulous and fiery, it's a hoot.
Webster’s sparkling version brings out all the cutting observations of an Irish outsider looking in on the absurdities of English society.
I certainly left in high spirits—an early Christmas treat.
This is a vibrant celebration of a playwright who has just as much to say to the 21st century as he did to his own.
The production is that, to be sure.
The result is outrageous, but only occasionally insightful and slightly less fun than it ought to be given the talent assembled on stage.
Big, bold, and beautiful, its star cast is matched by every element of its high-quality production value to create one of the strongest shows National Theatre have put on this year.
The Importance of Being Earnest is a wonderful, gloriously funny production that breathes fresh life into Wilde’s timeless farce.
It’s sharp, funny, and gloriously ridiculous—exactly as Wilde intended.
This interpretation navigates that with memorable panache.
They will, however, find something to enjoy in this cheeky and chaotic treat.
It's all frothy and entertaining but not as funny as it hopes it is.
The production is a must-see, bring a handbag and a friend!

cn.t: Critics praise this exuberantly camp, hot-pink production for its joyous queer reclamation of Wilde's classic, led by Ncuti Gatwa's charismatic performance. Most find it a delightful festive romp, though some purists feel the flamboyant staging overshadows the text.

vr.q: Oscar Wild triumphs despite production thanks to shoota, Hugh Skinner, and of course Sharon D. Clark doing justice to his clever, witty, perceptive script.
